mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz AMG GT S or GT C engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement M178 engine for a GT S or GT C typically costs between £4,500 and £16,500 depending on condition. Used units start from £4,500-£8,500, reconditioned from £8,000-£13,500, and fully rebuilt from £8,500-£16,500. Labour for supply & fit adds £800-£1,500 for AMG-specialist work.

mainEntity.name: Does the AMG GT S or GT C have a timing belt or timing chain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both the GT S and GT C use the M178 engine, which has a timing chain, not a belt. However, the M178 is known for timing chain stretch on higher-mileage units - a metallic rattling noise on cold start is the classic warning sign. Mercedes issued a service campaign (2021-03B) addressing timing chain guide wear on early M178 engines.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of engine problems in an AMG GT S or GT C?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common signs of engine problems in the GT S and GT C include: a rattling noise on cold start (timing chain stretch), loss of power or limp mode (turbo actuator failure), white steam from the engine bay or low coolant warnings (crossover pipe leak), and blue smoke on startup or after overrun (valve stem seal failure). If you experience any of these, have the car inspected immediately.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in an AMG GT S or GT C?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the car's condition and mileage. A GT S or GT C is typically worth £35,000-£80,000 - a rebuilt M178 engine (£8,500-£16,500) is usually well within the car's value and can be a worthwhile investment if the car is in good condition. For lower-value examples or those with multiple issues, a specialist repair may be more economical than a full replacement.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the GT S and GT C engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both the GT S and GT C use the same M178 4.0-litre V8 biturbo engine architecture, but with different power outputs and hardware. The GT S uses the M178 LS1 producing 510-522 hp with 650 Nm torque. The GT C uses the M178 producing 550-557 hp with 680 Nm torque - an increase achieved through revised turbochargers, a different ECU calibration, and a unique intake manifold. The GT C also features a wider rear track and active rear-axle steering, but the engine block and internals are largely shared.

mainEntity.name: What causes the AMG GT S or GT C to lose power?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power loss in the GT S and GT C is most commonly caused by turbo actuator failure, which sends the car into limp mode. Other causes include boost leaks from the hot-vee intercooler system, timing chain stretch causing cam timing drift, and carbon buildup on intake valves from the direct injection system. A diagnostic check with Mercedes STAR or compatible equipment is essential to identify the exact cause.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz AMG GT S / GT C - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The AMG GT S and GT C represent the performance-focused variants of the C190/R190 AMG GT range, positioned above the base GT and below the track-focused GT R. The GT S arrived at launch in 2015 as the higher-output option, while the GT C joined the range in 2016 as a mid-point between the GT S and GT R - also available as a roadster from 2018.

milestones.description: M178 LS1, 4.0L V8 biturbo, 510 hp - GT S launch; dry-sump oiling; 650 Nm torque; 0-62 mph in 3.8 seconds
M178, 4.0L V8 biturbo, 550 hp - GT C launch; positioned between GT S and GT R; 680 Nm torque; 0-62 mph in 3.7 seconds
Power bump for GT S to 522 hp; GT S remains in production alongside GT C
GT C Roadster launched; same 550 hp M178 engine; first open-top V8 AMG GT
Facelift with revised styling and updated engine management; power outputs unchanged
C190/R190 production ends; both GT S and GT C discontinued

problems.h4: M178 Timing Chain Stretch - Why the GT S and GT C Rattle on Cold Start
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz AMG GT S and GT C (M178 LS1 and M178, 2015-2021)
problems.rootCause: The single-row timing chain fitted to early M178 engines elongates under high thermal load, particularly on cars with frequent track use or aggressive downshifting. Chain slack allows the camshaft sprockets to jump timing, leading to valve-to-piston contact.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace timing chain, tensioner, guides, cam sprockets
repairOptions.longevity: Best done at first rattle; prevents catastrophic failure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove head, replace bent valves, lap seats, new gaskets
repairOptions.longevity: For engines with minor valve contact; adds 40-60k miles

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt engine with upgraded double-row chain and guides

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical AMG GT S or GT C is worth £35,000-£80,000 depending on condition and mileage. For vehicles under £40,000, a preventative chain replacement (£2,400-£3,200) is the better financial decision than a full engine replacement. For higher-value examples, a rebuilt M178 with warranty (£8,500-£16,500) offers peace of mind. Given the strong retained values of GT S and GT C models, replacement is usually justified for well-maintained cars.
problems.recommendation: If you hear a metallic rattling noise on cold start from the rear of the engine, act immediately. A preventative chain replacement at a specialist saves thousands compared to waiting for failure. Once the chain has slipped, replacement costs approach rebuild territory - at which point a fully rebuilt engine with upgraded internals makes better financial sense than repairing damaged heads.

problems.h4: M178 Turbocharger Actuator Failure - Boost Loss and Limp Mode
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz AMG GT S and GT C (M178 LS1 and M178, 2015-2021)
problems.rootCause: The hot-vee turbo placement exposes actuator electronics to extreme heat cycles, causing internal circuit board failure. Wastegate bushings wear, leading to boost pressure loss and eventual turbo overspin.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace electronic boost actuator only, recalibrate
repairOptions.longevity: Effective if caught before wastegate damage

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove turbos, replace bearings, wastegates, actuators
repairOptions.longevity: Suitable for cars with worn but not seized turbos

repairOptions.tier: Full Replacement - rebuilt engine with upgraded turbos
repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt engine with reinforced turbo seals and upgraded actuators
repairOptions.longevity: Recommended when both turbos have failed and engine has high miles

problems.recommendation: Turbo actuator failure is often misdiagnosed as a boost leak or vacuum issue. Get a diagnostic scan first. If only the actuator has failed, replacement is cost-effective. If wastegate bushings are also worn or turbos have oil seal leaks, a full turbo rebuild is the sensible middle ground. For high-mileage cars (80k+), investing in a rebuilt engine with upgraded turbo components protects your GT for years.
problems.cta: -> Get quotes for M178 turbo repair and replacement for your GT S / GT C

problems.group: M178 Hot-Vee Coolant Crossover Pipe Leak
problems.h4: M178 Hot-Vee Coolant Crossover Pipe Leak - The #1 Cooling System Failure
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz AMG GT S and GT C (M178 LS1 and M178, 2015-2021)
problems.rootCause: The plastic coolant crossover pipe mounted between the cylinder banks in the hot-vee degrades from sustained heat exposure. Once cracked, coolant leaks directly onto the hot turbo housings - creating steam, triggering low coolant warnings, and eventually causing overheating.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace plastic pipe with OEM or upgraded aluminium unit, refill coolant
repairOptions.longevity: Permanent fix if upgraded aluminium pipe used

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace crossover pipe, both intercooler bricks, coolant hoses
repairOptions.longevity: For cars with chronic coolant loss or evidence of overheating

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt engine with upgraded cooling system components
repairOptions.longevity: Required if engine overheated severely causing head gasket or ring failure

problems.recommendation: This is the most common coolant-related failure on M178 engines. Do not ignore low coolant warnings - driving with a cracked crossover pipe leads to rapid overheating and catastrophic engine damage. Replace the plastic pipe with an aftermarket aluminium unit as a preventative measure on any GT S or GT C over 40,000 miles. If caught early, the pipe replacement alone solves the problem for good.
